context.concept_name: Browser same-origin policy and the CORS/authentication boundary

coverage.learning_objective: Explain the browser origin boundary: classify same-origin and cross-origin calls to one API.

required_facts.statement: A browser origin is the combination of scheme, host and port; a difference in any of these makes two URLs cross-origin.
Browser same-origin restrictions limit a script's access to cross-origin responses unless the server permits that access through CORS.
An API must check access at its endpoints independently of the browser's cross-origin restrictions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A browser page and an API can be hosted at different addresses. Before blaming a rejected browser interaction on a bad login, separate two questions: are the addresses same-origin, and does the API permit this caller?

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A browser origin is the combination of scheme, host and port; a difference in any of these makes two URLs cross-origin.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Browser same-origin restrictions limit a script's access to cross-origin responses unless the server permits that access through CORS. An API must check access at its endpoints independently of the browser's cross-origin restrictions.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare hypothetical URLs https://shop.example:443/orders and https://shop.example:443/items. Their paths differ, but their scheme, host and port match, so they share an origin. Changing the second host to api.example makes it cross-origin. Changing only the port to 8443 also makes it cross-origin. Browser permission to read the API response and endpoint permission to access the requested information remain separate checks. A browser access restriction is not a substitute for the latter.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not equate a browser-origin check with authentication. Even when browser access is permitted, the API must independently check access.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Explain the browser origin boundary: classify same-origin and cross-origin calls to one API.

practice_anchor.objective: Classify calls from browser pages to https://shop.example:443/orders as same-origin or cross-origin by comparing scheme, host and port.
practice_anchor.success: Correctly classify https://shop.example:443/items as same-origin and http://shop.example:443/items, https://api.example:443/items, and https://shop.example:8443/items as cross-origin, identifying the differing origin component in each cross-origin case.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show one fixed API URL alongside browser-page URLs, with separate scheme, host and port columns and a same-origin or cross-origin classification. Make visible that a path change does not change the origin, while changing any origin component does. Keep browser response access and independent API access checks distinct.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Origins combine scheme, host and port; browser enforcement is not server authorization.
Stay within the current objective: Explain the browser origin boundary. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Distinguish browser access restrictions from API authentication.

coverage.learning_objective: Choose HTTP methods: select methods for one workflow.

required_facts.statement: A safe method has essentially read-only requested semantics; incidental effects such as logging do not make it unsafe.
A method is idempotent when multiple identical requests have the same intended server effect as one request, even if responses differ.
GET retrieves a selected representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without response content; both are safe and idempotent.
POST requests resource-specific processing of submitted content and is not generally idempotent.
PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state and DELETE removes its association with current functionality; both are idempotent but not safe.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders service needs operations for reading an order, processing a new submission, replacing a known order and removing it. Choosing a method means choosing intended effects, not merely selecting a convenient label.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A safe method has essentially read-only requested semantics; incidental effects such as logging do not make it unsafe.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A method is idempotent when multiple identical requests have the same intended server effect as one request, even if responses differ. GET retrieves a selected representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without response content; both are safe and idempotent. POST requests resource-specific processing of submitted content and is not generally idempotent. PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state and DELETE removes its association with current functionality; both are idempotent but not safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: For the same order workflow, compare reading a representation with replacing one. A read asks what the current representation is; replacement asks the server to establish the submitted target state. Both can be idempotent, but only the first is safe because the replacement requests a change. Next compare replacement with collection-specific creation processing. Repeating the replacement still requests the same target state, whereas POST is not generally idempotent. This comparison gives a useful method-selection discipline: describe the intended effect in plain language before choosing the method. Then describe identical repetition separately. Do not decide idempotency from whether the first and second replies happen to look alike.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Picture an order at /orders/42. A GET retrieves its representation; HEAD asks for the same semantics without response content. Neither requests a change to the order. A log entry produced during retrieval is incidental, so it does not contradict safety. Now imagine sending the same replacement with PUT twice. The intended state after the second replacement is the same as after the first: that is idempotency, even though the returned responses may differ. DELETE similarly need not return identical responses on repetition to remain idempotent. In contrast, a POST asking the collection to process a new order is not generally idempotent. Work through each proposed operation with two separate questions: does it request a state change, and would identical repetition have the same intended effect? This separates safe retrieval from idempotent changes without treating them as the same property.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Safe does not mean absolutely no side effects, and idempotent does not mean identical responses. PUT and DELETE illustrate why an idempotent operation can still be unsafe.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Choose HTTP methods: select methods for one workflow.

practice_anchor.objective: Select HTTP methods for an orders workflow: retrieve an order representation, request the same semantics without response content, process a new order submission, create or replace a known order's state, and remove its association with current functionality.
practice_anchor.success: Match the operations to GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, and DELETE respectively. Identify GET and HEAD as safe and idempotent, PUT and DELETE as idempotent but not safe, and POST as not generally idempotent. Judge repetition by intended server effects rather than identical responses, and treat incidental retrieval logging as compatible with safety.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the orders workflow's requested effects and repetition effects visible side by side for GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, and DELETE. Distinguish read-only requested semantics from state changes, and show why repeating the same replacement or removal preserves the intended effect even when responses differ.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Method semantics constrain effects and repetition.
Stay within the current objective: Choose HTTP methods. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine repeated operation effects.

coverage.learning_objective: Use representation metadata consistently: implement and test representation headers for one JSON operation.

required_facts.statement: Content-Type describes the media type of the associated representation, rather than the client's preferred response format.
Accept communicates acceptable response media types.
For a JSON exchange, send Content-Type: application/json for JSON content and Accept: application/json to request a JSON response, and inspect the response Content-Type separately.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A client sends an order as JSON and wants a JSON response. The outgoing body format, the response preference and the format actually returned are three different pieces of information.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Content-Type describes the media type of the associated representation, rather than the client's preferred response format.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Accept communicates acceptable response media types. For a JSON exchange, send Content-Type: application/json for JSON content and Accept: application/json to request a JSON response, and inspect the response Content-Type separately.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For this exchange, Content-Type: application/json describes the submitted JSON content. Accept: application/json states the acceptable response media type. When examining the reply, inspect its own Content-Type rather than assuming the request header already established the response format. Think of Content-Type as a label attached to content and Accept as a preference sent by the client. Reading those labels separately makes it easier to describe what was sent and what came back.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Content-Type is not the client's preferred response format; Accept carries that preference.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Use representation metadata consistently: implement and test representation headers for one JSON operation.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete the representation headers in a prepared HTTP request that sends an order as JSON, then check the returned representation using the response's own Content-Type.
practice_anchor.success: The request contains Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json. The learner identifies the returned media type from the response Content-Type, independently of the request headers.

live_code.required_skill: Edit raw HTTP representation headers and distinguish outgoing content metadata, response preferences and returned content metadata.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a prepared raw HTTP exchange for sending an order, with its JSON body and operation already supplied. Leave the two request representation headers unfinished and provide the response headers for separate inspection. No service implementation or test-library setup is required.
live_code.observable_success: Both completed request headers have the correct names and application/json values. The learner locates the response's separate Content-Type and uses that value, rather than the request's Accept or Content-Type, to identify the returned representation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make three distinct claims visible side by side: request Content-Type labels the submitted JSON, request Accept communicates acceptable response media types, and response Content-Type labels the content actually returned.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Client preferences and actual payload media types are different claims.
Stay within the current objective: Use representation metadata consistently. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Distinguish payload Content-Type from requested Accept negotiation.

Implementing an operation and writing endpoint integration tests require later concepts. Adapt the objective to completing raw HTTP headers in a prepared JSON order exchange and checking its supplied response metadata, without service declarations or test libraries.

context.concept_name: Practical Python type annotations for service interfaces

coverage.learning_objective: Annotate API data types: annotate one service function.

required_facts.statement: Annotate a function parameter with name: Type and its return value with -> Type; Python type hints alone do not enforce runtime validation.
Type | None permits None, while a default such as = None separately permits omitting a Python function argument.
list[str], set[str], tuple[int, str] and dict[str, int] annotate a list of strings, a set of strings, a two-element integer/string tuple and a string-to-integer dictionary respectively.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Before writing a service function, describe the values it accepts and returns. A reader should be able to tell whether an order note can be missing as a value, and whether the caller may omit the argument altogether.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Annotate a function parameter with name: Type and its return value with -> Type; Python type hints alone do not enforce runtime validation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Type | None permits None, while a default such as = None separately permits omitting a Python function argument. list[str], set[str], tuple[int, str] and dict[str, int] annotate a list of strings, a set of strings, a two-element integer/string tuple and a string-to-integer dictionary respectively.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Read an interface in two passes. First read the shapes: which parameter is a string, which result is an integer, and which collection has a declared element or key/value type? Then read defaults: which arguments can be omitted? For the note example, removing = None changes omission behavior without removing None from the admitted type. Removing | None changes the admitted values without itself establishing a default. These small edits answer different questions. Type hints help express the intended interface, but a runtime value does not become validated merely because the function declaration describes it. A reader should be able to explain both passes before relying on the interface.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Consider a parameter written note: str | None. It admits a string or None, but without a default the caller must still supply an argument. Writing note: str | None = None adds permission to omit it. These are different decisions: the type describes permitted values, while the default describes what happens when the argument is not provided. For an order summary, list[str] can describe item names, set[str] can describe tags, tuple[int, str] can describe a two-part identifier/name value, and dict[str, int] can describe counts keyed by name. Read each annotation aloud rather than treating the brackets as decoration. The return annotation after -> describes the function result in the same way. None of these descriptions, by themselves, proves that actual runtime values have been checked. Keep the interface description separate from a future validation mechanism.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a type hint does not add runtime validation. Also, allowing None is not the same as allowing an argument to be omitted.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Annotate API data types: annotate one service function.

practice_anchor.objective: Annotate an existing order-summary service function: item_names is a list of strings, tags is a set of strings, identifier_name is an integer/string pair, counts maps strings to integers, and note accepts a string or None and may be omitted. Annotate the returned counts as a string-to-integer dictionary.
practice_anchor.success: The function declares all parameter and return types correctly, and note has both a nullable annotation and a None default. The existing body remains unchanged; no runtime validation is added.

live_code.required_skill: Edit a function signature using parameter annotations, a return annotation, collection types, and a nullable type with a separate default.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide def order_summary(item_names, tags, identifier_name, counts, note): with the existing body return counts. Leave annotations and the note default absent. Supply the intended value shapes in the task description; require edits only to the signature.
live_code.observable_success: The edited signature is def order_summary(item_names: list[str], tags: set[str], identifier_name: tuple[int, str], counts: dict[str, int], note: str | None = None) -> dict[str, int]: and the body remains return counts.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the annotated order-summary signature visible, distinguishing parameter types, collection element or key/value types, the return type, and the separate roles of | None and = None.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Annotations describe shapes but do not themselves validate values.
Stay within the current objective: Annotate API data types. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Select annotations for required, nullable and collection values.

context.concept_name: Python classes and instances for service models

coverage.learning_objective: Represent state with classes and instances: implement two independent instances.

required_facts.statement: A class statement creates a class whose methods define behavior, and calling the class creates an instance.
Define __init__(self, ...) to initialize an instance and assign self.attribute to store that instance's state; an instance method receives that instance as its first argument.
Instance variables hold data specific to each instance, while class variables are shared by instances of the class.
A mutable class variable can be shared unintentionally; initialize a fresh mutable value on self inside __init__ when instances need independent values.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two order drafts need independent state. A class gives them a shared definition of behavior, but the two instances must not accidentally share a mutable collection intended to belong to just one draft.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A class statement creates a class whose methods define behavior, and calling the class creates an instance.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define __init__(self, ...) to initialize an instance and assign self.attribute to store that instance's state; an instance method receives that instance as its first argument. Instance variables hold data specific to each instance, while class variables are shared by instances of the class. A mutable class variable can be shared unintentionally; initialize a fresh mutable value on self inside __init__ when instances need independent values.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Use the two drafts to test your understanding of ownership. Start with each draft intended to have an empty item collection. Change only the first draft and ask what state the second should have under the requirement of independence. If both are using one mutable class variable, that requirement is not met by merely calling the class twice. The corrective declaration is a fresh mutable value assigned on self inside initialization. Methods can be shared as class-defined behavior while their self argument identifies which instance is being operated on. This is the central separation: one definition of behavior can serve several instances whose state is meant to differ.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Draft is the class and draft_a and draft_b are two instances created by calling it twice. Its __init__ method assigns an item collection to self.items. Because initialization creates a fresh collection on each self, adding an item to draft_a belongs to that instance's state rather than to a shared class collection. Compare that with placing one mutable items value on the class: both instances can then see the shared value. Follow the ownership, not just the attribute name. The class defines the methods, and a method receives the particular instance as its first argument when operating on that instance. A useful reasoning exercise is to draw two instance boxes and write the intended state inside each. If both boxes point to one class-level collection despite requiring independence, the model does not match the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Having two instances does not make every attribute independent. A mutable class variable can still be shared; create fresh instance state inside __init__ when independence is required.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Represent state with classes and instances: implement two independent instances.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement Draft so that draft_a and draft_b each start with an independent empty items list, then add an item only to draft_a.
practice_anchor.success: Both instances are created by calling Draft. Each receives a fresh items list inside __init__; after adding an item to draft_a.items, draft_b.items remains empty.

live_code.required_skill: Define a class and initialize independent mutable state on each instance.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an unfinished Draft class and space to create draft_a and draft_b. Require items to start empty on each instance, without supplying a shared class-level list.
live_code.observable_success: Inspect draft_a.items and draft_b.items after appending one string item only to draft_a.items. The first contains that item and the second remains empty; the implementation assigns a fresh list to self.items inside __init__.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show Draft as the shared definition of behavior and draft_a and draft_b as separate instances. Contrast both instances pointing to one class-level items list with each instance pointing to its own list created inside __init__.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Classes define behavior; instances own state.
Stay within the current objective: Represent state with classes and instances. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Distinguish instance from class state.

coverage.learning_objective: Use context-managed cleanup: manage one acquired resource.

required_facts.statement: Use with manager as resource: followed by an indented block to enter a managed resource scope.
If __enter__ returns successfully, the with statement calls __exit__ when the block exits normally or through an exception.
__exit__ receives exception details on exceptional exit and can suppress the exception by returning a true value; cleanup does not itself imply suppression.
Using with open(...) as file closes the file after the block, including when an exception occurs.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A service-related script reads a file, but the work inside that reading step might fail. The resource boundary should describe cleanup on both the successful path and the exceptional path.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use with manager as resource: followed by an indented block to enter a managed resource scope.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: If __enter__ returns successfully, the with statement calls __exit__ when the block exits normally or through an exception. __exit__ receives exception details on exceptional exit and can suppress the exception by returning a true value; cleanup does not itself imply suppression. Using with open(...) as file closes the file after the block, including when an exception occurs.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: The boundary can be understood without designing a custom manager. Mark three points in the file example: successful entry, execution inside the block, and departure from the block. Departing normally and departing because of an exception both lead to file closure. For a general manager, a true __exit__ result can suppress an exception; that decision belongs to the manager and is separate from releasing the resource. Therefore a cleanup trace should not silently replace a failed operation with a successful one. State both outcomes explicitly: the resource exited its managed scope, and the exception was either propagated or intentionally suppressed under the manager behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: In with open(...) as file, the indented block is the managed scope. Trace entry first: the manager enters successfully and supplies the resource used by the block. Trace normal exit next: leaving the block closes the file. Finally trace an exception raised while the block is using it: the managed exit still closes the file. That is the cleanup guarantee to rely on, conditional on successful entry. For a general manager, __exit__ also receives information about an exception and may suppress it by returning a true value. Therefore ask two questions separately: was the resource released, and was the failure propagated? Releasing a file does not itself mean that the failed work succeeded or that the exception was suppressed. Keep the useful work inside the indented resource boundary so that the scope is visible to the reader.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Cleanup and exception suppression are separate behaviors. Successful entry guarantees an exit call, not that exceptions disappear.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Use context-managed cleanup: manage one acquired resource.

context.concept_name: Cooperative concurrency with async and await

coverage.learning_objective: Reason about cooperative coroutine execution and conditional suspension at await: trace one coroutine with an immediately completing await and an await on a pending I/O operation, identifying where another runnable task can execute.

required_facts.statement: Calling an async def function produces a coroutine; awaiting it runs it and returns its result when it completes.
An event loop uses cooperative scheduling, running one task at a time and allowing other tasks to run while a task waits on a pending future.
An await can complete without suspension when its awaited operation completes immediately; the presence of await alone does not establish a switch to another task.
When a future awaited by a suspended task completes, execution of that task's coroutine resumes.
To trace suspension concretely, mark await asyncio.sleep(...) as a suspension point; sleep suspends the current task, including when its delay is zero.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An asynchronous service task can contain several awaits without letting another task run at every one. To reason about concurrency, identify actual suspension rather than simply counting await keywords.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Calling an async def function produces a coroutine; awaiting it runs it and returns its result when it completes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: An event loop uses cooperative scheduling, running one task at a time and allowing other tasks to run while a task waits on a pending future. An await can complete without suspension when its awaited operation completes immediately; the presence of await alone does not establish a switch to another task. When a future awaited by a suspended task completes, execution of that task's coroutine resumes. To trace suspension concretely, mark await asyncio.sleep(...) as a suspension point; sleep suspends the current task, including when its delay is zero.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A useful execution sketch has two columns: current task and waiting condition. An immediately completed await leaves no pending wait to justify a handover. A suspended await has a pending future, so another runnable task may use the event loop while the first waits. When that future completes, the first task can resume. This sketch does not require claiming exactly which other task runs; it identifies the opportunity for cooperative scheduling. For asyncio.sleep, explicitly mark suspension even when the delay is zero. That exception to a casual "zero means immediate" intuition is why a careful trace uses documented operation behavior rather than guessing from the numeric argument.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Follow task A through an immediately completing coroutine and then through await asyncio.sleep(0). Calling the async function first creates a coroutine; awaiting it runs that coroutine and obtains its result. If that work completes immediately, A can continue without switching tasks. The sleep is different: even a zero delay suspends A, giving another runnable task an opportunity to execute. While A is suspended, the event loop still runs one task at a time; cooperative scheduling is not several tasks executing simultaneously in that loop. When the future A was waiting for completes, A resumes its coroutine. On paper, mark each operation as either completing immediately or waiting on a pending future, then mark only the latter as a possible handover, with sleep explicitly treated as suspension. This produces a more accurate execution trace than drawing an automatic switch after every await.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An await is not proof that another task ran. Immediately completing awaited work can return without suspension; asyncio.sleep suspends even with delay zero.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Reason about cooperative coroutine execution and conditional suspension at await: trace one coroutine with an immediately completing await and an await on a pending I/O operation, identifying where another runnable task can execute.

practice_anchor.objective: Annotate supplied coroutine code for task A: trace an immediately completing await, an await on a supplied pending I/O future, and await asyncio.sleep(0). Identify suspension points, opportunities for another runnable task to execute, and where A continues after the pending future completes.
practice_anchor.success: The annotations distinguish coroutine creation from execution, show no required handover at the immediately completing await, mark the pending-future await and zero-delay sleep as suspension points, and place A's continuation after its awaited future becomes ready without asserting an exact task execution order.

live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide task A's coroutine code and a supplied execution harness, with an immediately completing coroutine, a pending I/O future, and asyncio.sleep(0). Learners annotate existing code; they do not construct the I/O operation, future, or scheduling harness.
live_code.observable_success: Source comments correctly mark immediate completion, suspension, possible execution of another runnable task, and continuation after future completion. The zero-delay sleep is explicitly marked as suspension, and no comment claims that every await switches tasks.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make task A's execution trace visible alongside its waiting condition: coroutine creation, immediate awaited completion without suspension, suspension on a pending future, another runnable task's opportunity to execute, and A's continuation when the future completes. Separately mark asyncio.sleep(0) as suspending without claiming an exact scheduling order.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Await yields control only when the awaited operation suspends; an immediately completing coroutine can return without suspending the current task..
Stay within the current objective: Reason about cooperative coroutine execution and conditional suspension at await. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Predict whether an await continues immediately or suspends the current task, and how a suspended task resumes when its awaited operation is ready.

coverage.learning_objective: Understand decorators as callable wrappers: write and inspect one simple callable wrapper.

required_facts.statement: A decorator expression is evaluated when a function is defined, called with the function object, and its returned value is bound to the function name.
@decorate above def function(...): applies decoration roughly like function = decorate(function).
A callable wrapper can be built by defining an inner function that calls the supplied function and returning that inner function from the decorator.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You want to add behavior around a service callable without rewriting the callable itself. A decorator lets another callable receive the function and determine what its name will refer to afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A decorator expression is evaluated when a function is defined, called with the function object, and its returned value is bound to the function name.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: @decorate above def function(...): applies decoration roughly like function = decorate(function). A callable wrapper can be built by defining an inner function that calls the supplied function and returning that inner function from the decorator.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Read @decorate above a function definition as roughly function = decorate(function). The decorator receives the function object, not the result of running that function with service data. A wrapper decorator can define an inner function that calls the supplied function and then return that inner function. The name now refers to what the decorator returned. Trace this in two stages: definition time applies the decorator and establishes the binding; a later call uses that bound value. If the returned value is the wrapper, the later call goes through the wrapper to the original callable. This distinction matters when reading service registration code: seeing @ above def means something happens while the function is defined, not just each time a request-related call is made. Keep the returned value in the trace rather than assuming decoration leaves the original binding untouched.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A decorator is not merely a comment attached to a function. Its returned value becomes the binding for the function name.

context.concept_name: Isolated Python environments and compatible dependency installation

coverage.learning_objective: Install service dependencies in an isolated environment: create an environment and install a compatible dependency set.

required_facts.statement: A virtual environment has a particular Python installation and its own installed packages, allowing applications to use different dependency versions.
Create an environment with python -m venv .venv and activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on Unix or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows.
Use python -m pip install package within the environment to install a dependency, and python -m pip show package to inspect its installed version and location.
Check which python on Unix or where python on Windows to confirm that the interpreter path belongs to the activated environment.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two backend projects may need different package versions. Installing everything into whichever interpreter happens to be on the machine makes it difficult to tell which project is using which dependencies.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A virtual environment has a particular Python installation and its own installed packages, allowing applications to use different dependency versions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Create an environment with python -m venv .venv and activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on Unix or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows. Use python -m pip install package within the environment to install a dependency, and python -m pip show package to inspect its installed version and location. Check which python on Unix or where python on Windows to confirm that the interpreter path belongs to the activated environment.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the evidence in the environment exercise. The interpreter path tells you which Python command the shell resolves. Package inspection tells you the version and location visible through that interpreter. Together they make the dependency namespace concrete. If a teammate reports another installed version, first compare the two interpreter paths and package locations rather than assuming the project declaration changed. The environment is tied to a particular Python installation and has its own installed packages, so two applications can use different dependency versions. This explanation establishes environment isolation; recording declarations for reconstruction is a separate later task.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Create .venv for one project, activate it using the command for the operating system, and then inspect the interpreter path. On Unix, which python should point into that environment; on Windows, use where python. Only after identifying the interpreter should you install a dependency with python -m pip install package. Then inspect it with python -m pip show package, checking both version and location. The location is useful evidence that this project is using its own installed package rather than another environment's copy. Repeat the same reasoning for the second project: its environment has its own installed packages and a particular Python installation. Activation and installation are steps in establishing that boundary; the interpreter-path check confirms which boundary your current shell commands are actually using.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not treat an activation command alone as evidence that you inspected the right interpreter. Confirm the path, and inspect package version and location.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Install service dependencies in an isolated environment: create an environment and install a compatible dependency set.

practice_anchor.objective: Create and activate .venv for one project, verify its interpreter path, and install a supplied dependency set compatible with the available Python installation. Inspect each installed dependency's version and location.
practice_anchor.success: The interpreter path belongs to .venv, installation succeeds for every supplied dependency, and package inspection reports each dependency's installed version and a location inside .venv rather than the host package location.

live_code.required_skill: Use terminal commands to create an isolated Python environment, select its interpreter, install supplied compatible dependencies, and inspect isolation evidence.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a project directory without .venv, an available Python installation, and dependency names already checked for mutual compatibility with that installation. Supply the host interpreter path and host package location as comparison evidence. Explain that package in the taught commands is replaced with each supplied dependency name.
live_code.observable_success: The learner creates and activates .venv using the appropriate operating-system commands. which python or where python resolves to its interpreter. Repeated python -m pip install package commands succeed, and python -m pip show package reports each installed version and an environment-local location.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the host interpreter path and package location visibly distinct from the activated .venv interpreter path and installed package locations, with inspected package versions alongside them.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: An environment isolates an interpreter's dependency namespace.
Stay within the current objective: Install service dependencies in an isolated environment. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Demonstrate interpreter and dependency isolation from the host.

context.concept_name: ASGI server and application request lifecycle

coverage.learning_objective: Explain ASGI lifecycle: trace one request.

required_facts.statement: An ASGI server handles the network connection and invokes an application callable through the ASGI interface.
The application callable has the shape async def app(scope, receive, send), where scope describes the connection and receive and send exchange protocol events.
Trace the application receiving http.request events through receive(), then sending http.response.start with status and headers followed by http.response.body through send().

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: When an HTTP request reaches a Python application, the network server and the application have different responsibilities. ASGI is the interface through which the server invokes the application and exchanges protocol events.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: An ASGI server handles the network connection and invokes an application callable through the ASGI interface.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: The application callable has the shape async def app(scope, receive, send), where scope describes the connection and receive and send exchange protocol events. Trace the application receiving http.request events through receive(), then sending http.response.start with status and headers followed by http.response.body through send().

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the scope and the event stream distinct in the drawing. Scope describes the connection passed to the application, whereas receive and send are used to exchange protocol events. For the response, status and headers belong to http.response.start, followed by body content through http.response.body. The order in that response trace matters: the metadata event and body event are not interchangeable names for a single application return. The network connection stays in the server box, and the ASGI callable stays in the application box. Understanding those roles is enough here; the learner does not need to implement connection handling to explain the request lifecycle.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace one request across the boundary. The server handles the network connection and invokes the async application callable. Its scope describes the connection; receive and send are the event-exchange callables supplied to it. The application receives http.request events through receive(). To produce its reply, it sends http.response.start containing status and headers, followed by http.response.body. Draw those events as arrows rather than treating the handler's return value as the entire network lifecycle. The start event and body event have different jobs: one establishes response metadata and the other carries body content. Keeping the server outside the application box also clarifies who owns the network connection and who participates in the ASGI protocol. You need to understand this event boundary without implementing a server from scratch.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: The application callable is not the component that directly owns all network handling. The ASGI server handles the connection and invokes the application through the interface.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Explain ASGI lifecycle: trace one request.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete async def app(scope, receive, send) to trace one HTTP request: await the supplied receive callable, then send response metadata followed by body content using the supplied send callable.
practice_anchor.success: The application receives the supplied http.request event and sends http.response.start with the supplied status and headers before sending http.response.body with the supplied body. The trace identifies network handling and application invocation as server responsibilities.

live_code.required_skill: Use async and await to exchange ASGI protocol events in request-response order while keeping server and application responsibilities distinct.
allowed_syntax: String literals for event types and keys
Integer literals for the supplied status
List and tuple literals for the supplied headers
Bytes literals for the supplied headers and body
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the app(scope, receive, send) signature, supplied scope, and simulated receive and send callables. receive supplies one complete http.request event; send records outgoing events. Supply fixed status, headers, and body literals so the learner only completes the event exchange, without implementing network handling or choosing a status.
live_code.observable_success: The supplied trace records receive() yielding http.request, then send() receiving http.response.start containing the supplied status and headers, then send() receiving http.response.body containing the supplied body. The application contains no network-handling implementation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show separate server and application boxes. Place the network connection and application invocation in the server box; show scope passed to app(scope, receive, send), an incoming http.request through receive(), and outgoing http.response.start with status and headers followed by http.response.body through send().

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Servers adapt traffic to application protocol lifecycle.
Stay within the current objective: Explain ASGI lifecycle. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Locate server and application responsibilities.

context.concept_name: Local password hashing and credential verification without an OAuth password grant

coverage.learning_objective: Verify passwords securely: use one established hashing library.

required_facts.statement: Password storage should use password hashing rather than plaintext storage or reversible encryption.
Salts distinguish password hashes, while an adjustable work factor increases the cost of password guessing.
Create PasswordHash.recommended() from pwdlib, store the result of its hash(password) method, and verify a submitted password with verify(plain_password, stored_hash).

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A local login check needs to compare a submitted password with stored verification material. The stored value should not be the password itself or an encrypted value intended to be decrypted later.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Password storage should use password hashing rather than plaintext storage or reversible encryption.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Salts distinguish password hashes, while an adjustable work factor increases the cost of password guessing. Create PasswordHash.recommended() from pwdlib, store the result of its hash(password) method, and verify a submitted password with verify(plain_password, stored_hash).

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Create a PasswordHash.recommended() instance from pwdlib. When registering a hypothetical local account, store the result of hash(password). During a later login attempt, pass the submitted plain password and stored hash to verify(plain_password, stored_hash). Salt distinguishes hashes, while the adjustable work factor increases guessing cost. These support password verification without making reversible password storage the goal. Use synthetic passwords in an exercise and keep attention on what is stored and what is supplied to the verification call.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Password hashing is not reversible encryption. Verification compares a submission with a stored hash rather than recovering the original password.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Verify passwords securely: use one established hashing library.

practice_anchor.objective: Use pwdlib to create a recommended password hasher, hash a synthetic password, and verify matching and nonmatching submissions against the stored hash.
practice_anchor.success: The stored value is the result of hash(password), and verify(plain_password, stored_hash) returns true for the matching submission and false for a different submission.

live_code.required_skill: Instantiate PasswordHash.recommended() and use its hash and verify methods with the correct arguments.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an isolated environment with pwdlib available and a synthetic password assigned to password. Leave creation of password_hash, assignment of stored_hash, and verification results for the learner.
live_code.observable_success: Execution produces stored_hash through password_hash.hash(password). Two verification result variables hold true for the original synthetic password and false for a different synthetic password, with the stored hash passed as the second argument.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the recommended hasher instance, synthetic input password, stored hash, and verification argument order visible in annotated code, alongside matching and nonmatching Boolean results.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Passwords require one-way work-factor-based verification.
Stay within the current objective: Verify passwords securely. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify safe storage and verification designs.

coverage.learning_objective: Map entities to database tables: map one entity with a primary key.

required_facts.statement: A mapped class associates Python attributes with a database table's columns; first create the shared base with class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass, then inherit mapped entities from Base and declare attributes with Mapped[Type] and mapped_column(...).
Declare a primary-key attribute with mapped_column(primary_key=True) to identify persistent rows.
__tablename__ gives the table name in a declarative mapped class, while mapped_column arguments and annotations describe column details.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order needs a Python representation tied to a persistent database row. ORM mapping establishes that association, including which attribute identifies the row.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A mapped class associates Python attributes with a database table's columns; first create the shared base with class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass, then inherit mapped entities from Base and declare attributes with Mapped[Type] and mapped_column(...).

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a primary-key attribute with mapped_column(primary_key=True) to identify persistent rows. __tablename__ gives the table name in a declarative mapped class, while mapped_column arguments and annotations describe column details.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the mapping as a declaration before imagining any stored state. The shared Base establishes the base used by mapped entities. The entity subclass names a table with __tablename__ and describes its column-associated attributes through Mapped and mapped_column. The primary-key declaration is the part that identifies persistent rows. In the order example, label these three concerns separately: class inheritance, table naming and row identity. A familiar attribute name such as id is not the explanation by itself; the primary_key=True declaration supplies the mapping role. This gives later persistence operations a model to work with without pretending the mapping declaration has already completed those operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the shared declarative Base, then define an Order entity inheriting from it. Give it a __tablename__ such as orders and describe its attributes with Mapped[Type] and mapped_column(...). For the identity attribute, mapped_column(primary_key=True) marks the persistent row identity. Mentally draw one Python attribute next to its database column: the annotation and column arguments describe the mapping, while the primary-key declaration identifies rows. Do not confuse an ordinary instance having a field called id with a mapping that declares a primary key. In this exercise the goal is the entity-to-table association itself. You can inspect the declarations and explain the table name, attributes and key before moving on to later operations that retrieve or modify rows. This keeps mapping separate from performing a database write.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Constructing a mapped class definition does not by itself describe a completed write. Here the task is to declare the attribute-to-column association and row identity.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Map entities to database tables: map one entity with a primary key.

practice_anchor.success: Order inherits from Base, names the orders table, and declares id using Mapped[int] and mapped_column(primary_key=True).

live_code.observable_success: The completed declarations contain Base inheriting from DeclarativeBase, Order inheriting from Base, __tablename__ set to "orders", and id annotated as Mapped[int] with mapped_column(primary_key=True).

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the Base and Order declarations with annotations distinguishing shared-base inheritance, the orders table name, the id-to-column association, and primary_key=True as the persistent-row identity declaration.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Entity state is associated with a persistent row identified by a key..
Stay within the current objective: Map entities to database tables. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine persistent row identity and columns.

coverage.learning_objective: Handle CORS preflight: verify one preflight exchange.

required_facts.statement: A browser preflights some cross-origin requests with OPTIONS to ask whether the intended method and headers are permitted before sending the actual request.
A CORS preflight includes Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; Access-Control-Request-Headers identifies requested headers when applicable.

Verify a preflight by sending the caller's Origin and intended method and headers, then comparing Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers with that request.
A credentialed cross-origin response requires an explicit allowed origin rather than * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A browser wants to make a cross-origin call using a particular method and headers. For some requests it first asks whether that intended call is permitted, before sending the actual request.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A browser preflights some cross-origin requests with OPTIONS to ask whether the intended method and headers are permitted before sending the actual request.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A CORS preflight includes Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; Access-Control-Request-Headers identifies requested headers when applicable. Verify a preflight by sending the caller's Origin and intended method and headers, then comparing Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers with that request. A credentialed cross-origin response requires an explicit allowed origin rather than * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace an OPTIONS preflight for a hypothetical client origin https://shop.example that wants to use PUT with a content-type header. The preflight carries Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method, plus Access-Control-Request-Headers when requested headers need to be identified. Compare the reply's Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers with those requested values. This is a comparison between an intended call and the server's browser-access permission, not the actual operation's business response. If the cross-origin response is credentialed, look for an explicit allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true rather than accepting a wildcard origin. Label the preflight and actual request separately in a trace so that a successful permission negotiation is not mistaken for completion of the intended operation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Not every cross-origin request is preflighted. Also, a wildcard allowed origin is not the required origin response for a credentialed exchange.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Handle CORS preflight: verify one preflight exchange.

practice_anchor.success: Compare Access-Control-Allow-Origin with https://shop.example, check that Access-Control-Allow-Methods permits PUT, and check that Access-Control-Allow-Headers permits content-type. Record whether the preflight permits the intended request without treating permission as completion of PUT. For the supplied credentialed-response check, require the explicit allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; reject * as the allowed origin.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the browser's OPTIONS request with its origin, intended method, and requested header; align those values with the server's corresponding allow headers. Show the actual PUT as a separate, conditional next step, and annotate the explicit-origin and allow-credentials requirements for a credentialed response.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Preflight negotiates browser permission before an operation.
Stay within the current objective: Handle CORS preflight. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.

context.concept_name: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses

coverage.learning_objective: Select HTTP statuses: assign one resource's statuses.

required_facts.statement: HTTP status classes distinguish informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx and server error 5xx outcomes.
Use 200 for a successful request, 201 when the request creates a resource, and 204 for successful completion with no response content.

400 denotes a perceived client request error, 401 lacks valid authentication credentials, 403 refuses fulfillment, 404 does not find or disclose the target, and 409 conflicts with current resource state.
500 denotes an unexpected server condition and 503 denotes temporary inability to handle the request, such as overload or maintenance.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders API needs clients to distinguish a successful creation, an absent order and an unexpected service failure. Status codes communicate those outcomes before the client interprets the body.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: HTTP status classes distinguish informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx and server error 5xx outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use 200 for a successful request, 201 when the request creates a resource, and 204 for successful completion with no response content. 400 denotes a perceived client request error, 401 lacks valid authentication credentials, 403 refuses fulfillment, 404 does not find or disclose the target, and 409 conflicts with current resource state. 500 denotes an unexpected server condition and 503 denotes temporary inability to handle the request, such as overload or maintenance.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A useful review begins with the meaning of the outcome, not a memorized list of favorite codes. Ask whether the request succeeded, whether a client request problem prevents fulfillment, or whether an unexpected or temporary server condition prevents handling. Then distinguish cases within the class. Creation differs from retrieval; absent valid credentials differ from refusal; a conflict with current state differs from not finding or disclosing the target. These meanings let the same orders workflow produce intentionally different statuses. The response body can elaborate, but the status already conveys a defined outcome category. Do not use a successful status simply because a JSON body was produced.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Build an outcome table for a hypothetical order workflow. Successful retrieval can use 200; successful creation can use 201; successful completion with no response content can use 204. If the requested order is not found or disclosed, 404 fits that outcome. If a write conflicts with the current state, consider the declared 409 outcome. Keep credential problems separate from refusal: 401 means valid authentication credentials are lacking, whereas 403 denotes refusal to fulfill. Now compare unexpected failure with temporary inability to handle requests: those correspond to 500 and 503 respectively. First choose the outcome class, then the particular meaning within it. This avoids choosing every rejection as a generic 400 or every operational problem as the same server error. The table is about HTTP meaning, not a promise that a particular framework declaration will automatically produce each status.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Client errors and server errors convey different outcome classes. A no-content success is 204, not a promise of a response body.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Select HTTP statuses: assign one resource's statuses.

practice_anchor.objective: Assign integer HTTP statuses to named variables representing successful and failed outcomes for the hypothetical orders workflow, without implementing request handling.
practice_anchor.success: The order outcome assignments use 200 for successful retrieval, 201 for creation, 204 for successful completion without response content, 400 for a perceived client request error, 401 for missing valid authentication credentials, 403 for refusal, 404 for an order not found or disclosed, 409 for a current-state conflict, 500 for an unexpected server condition, and 503 for temporary inability to handle the request.
