Associate each variable with its stated orders-workflow outcome; learners replace only the integer values.
live_code.observable_success: The ten variables hold 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 500, and 503 respectively, using only integer assignments and no request-handling implementation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make an orders outcome table visible with columns for outcome, HTTP status class, and selected status. Contrast retrieval, creation, no-content success, request error, missing valid credentials, refusal, target not found or disclosed, current-state conflict, unexpected server failure, and temporary unavailability. Include a compact key for all five status classes, including informational and redirection outcomes.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Status communicates exchange outcome class.
Stay within the current objective: Select HTTP statuses. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Choose statuses matching outcomes.

context.concept_name: Pydantic V2 model construction and input conversion

coverage.learning_objective: Construct validated models: define one request model.

required_facts.statement: Define a Pydantic model by subclassing BaseModel and declaring typed fields, then construct it with Model(field=value, ...) or validate data with Model.model_validate(data).
Pydantic validation can convert compatible inputs to declared types; its default validation is not a guarantee that input values already had those types.
Inputs that cannot satisfy a model raise ValidationError with details about the failed fields.
A field without a default is required; a declared default supplies its value when it is omitted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Incoming order data needs a declared shape. Model validation turns compatible input into a model or explains why the input cannot satisfy that shape; it is not merely a test that the original values already had exact types.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Define a Pydantic model by subclassing BaseModel and declaring typed fields, then construct it with Model(field=value, ...) or validate data with Model.model_validate(data).

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Pydantic validation can convert compatible inputs to declared types; its default validation is not a guarantee that input values already had those types. Inputs that cannot satisfy a model raise ValidationError with details about the failed fields. A field without a default is required; a declared default supplies its value when it is omitted.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect presence and conversion separately in the order example. A required quantity omitted from input has a different problem from a present quantity that cannot satisfy the integer field. A defaulted note omitted from input follows a third path: the declared default supplies its value. Now inspect compatible conversion: the validated model can contain the declared type even though the original input did not already have it. Explaining all these cases prevents the phrase "validation passed" from hiding what validation actually established. It established a model satisfying the declared shape, with defaults and compatible conversion where applicable, not a historical assertion about every original input type.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an OrderInput model with a required quantity: int field and a note field that has a declared default. Construct it from data with quantity supplied and note omitted. The missing note receives its default, while quantity must be present because it has no default. Try a compatible value that can be converted to the declared quantity type, then try one that cannot satisfy that type. The former illustrates conversion during validation; the latter raises ValidationError with field details. Compare those outcomes with omitting quantity entirely. All three cases answer different questions: was the field supplied, can its value satisfy the type, and what should omission produce when a default exists? Read the resulting model as validated output, not as proof that every input value started with the same type as the corresponding field.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Ordinary model validation can convert compatible input values. An integer in the resulting model does not prove that the original input was already an integer.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Construct validated models: define one request model.

media.group_title: Constructing models with required fields and defaults

segments.label: Define typed fields, construct a model, and apply defaults
segments.summary: A User class inherits from BaseModel and declares username and email as string fields. Neither field has a default, so constructing User without arguments produces validation errors identifying both missing fields. Supplying strings for both fields succeeds. Adding bio with an empty-string default and is_active with a True default allows those fields to be omitted during construction; the resulting instance receives their declared defaults. Here, “optional fields” means fields that may be omitted because they have defaults.

bridge_note.before: Watch how typed declarations determine required fields and how defaults supply omitted values. The clip calls defaulted fields “optional”; here, that means omission is allowed, not that any value is accepted.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates construction, missing-field errors, and defaults, but not compatible input conversion or model_validate. The text covers those gaps and explains that incompatible supplied values also raise ValidationError.

practice_anchor.objective: Define a standalone OrderInput request-data model with required quantity: int and note: str defaulting to an empty string. Construct it with quantity="3", and validate equivalent dictionary data with OrderInput.model_validate.
practice_anchor.success: Both resulting instances contain integer quantity 3 and an empty-string note. The quantity declaration has no default, while note has its declared default.

live_code.required_skill: Declare typed BaseModel fields and construct validated instances from keyword arguments and dictionary data.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the BaseModel import and an unfinished OrderInput declaration using only the quantity and note field names; leave field declarations and construction expressions for the learner.
live_code.observable_success: Inspection of the two instances shows quantity as integer 3 and note as an empty string; inspection of the class declaration shows quantity without a default and note with a default.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the OrderInput field declarations visible beside inputs and outcomes: quantity="3" becomes integer 3, omitted note receives its default, omitted quantity fails, and quantity="many" produces a field validation error.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Construction converts and validates against a shape.
Stay within the current objective: Construct validated models. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine accepted values and conversions.

coverage.learning_objective: Declare reproducible service dependencies: install a service in a clean environment from dependency files.

required_facts.statement: python -m pip freeze reports installed packages and versions, and its output can be saved to requirements.txt for a dependency declaration.
Install declared dependencies in an environment with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt.
Reconstruct the environment from committed dependency declarations rather than relying on packages installed manually in another environment; the build stage obtains the declared dependencies.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A teammate needs to reconstruct the backend environment without guessing what you installed locally. The dependency declaration becomes part of the project's build contract.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: python -m pip freeze reports installed packages and versions, and its output can be saved to requirements.txt for a dependency declaration.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Install declared dependencies in an environment with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. Reconstruct the environment from committed dependency declarations rather than relying on packages installed manually in another environment; the build stage obtains the declared dependencies.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect installed versions with python -m pip freeze and save the output as requirements.txt for the declaration. Commit that declaration, then use python -m pip install -r requirements.txt in the environment being reconstructed. The important comparison is between the declared packages and the packages obtained for the build, not between two developers' memories of installation steps. A package that happens to be installed in your working environment is not a reliable substitute for a committed declaration. Think through a handoff: the teammate has the project and its declared dependencies, but not your local environment. The build stage must obtain those dependencies from the declaration. This exercise concerns reconstructing the installed dependency set; do not quietly broaden it into a claim that every external condition of a service is reproduced by freeze alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A successful run on one manually prepared environment is not a dependency declaration. Reconstruct from the committed declaration, not accidental local installations.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Declare reproducible service dependencies: install a service in a clean environment from dependency files.

media.group_title: Capture dependencies for a reproducible handoff

segments.label: Save installed dependencies to requirements.txt
segments.summary: The demonstration creates and activates an isolated Python environment, installs example packages, and redirects pip freeze output into requirements.txt. The resulting declaration includes dependencies of the explicitly installed packages, which explains the additional entries. Sharing this file lets another person install the listed dependencies in their own environment.

bridge_note.before: Watch how installed packages become a requirements.txt declaration. The clip uses bare pip in an activated environment; Devspace uses python -m pip to explicitly select the environment's Python interpreter.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains sharing the declaration, but omits the install -r command and committed-declaration build workflow. The text supplies both: install from requirements.txt and have the build obtain committed dependencies.

practice_anchor.objective: Install the service's declared dependencies in a provided clean, isolated environment using the committed requirements.txt file.
practice_anchor.success: The declared dependencies install successfully, and the installed package versions satisfy the committed requirements.txt entries without relying on packages from the original working environment.

live_code.required_skill: Run dependency installation from a requirements file and inspect installed versions using the environment's Python interpreter.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an active, clean isolated environment and the service's committed requirements.txt, with compatible package versions available for installation. Keep the declaration unchanged during reconstruction.
live_code.observable_success: The installation command completes successfully. The installed versions reported by python -m pip freeze satisfy every entry in the provided requirements.txt.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the committed requirements.txt entries and installed package versions visible side by side, with the installation command shown, so learners can verify reconstruction from the declaration.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Dependency declarations are part of the build contract, not memory of local installations.
Stay within the current objective: Declare reproducible service dependencies. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Recreate a compatible dependency set from committed declarations.

context.concept_name: Python package organization for a service

coverage.learning_objective: Organize an importable package: arrange one runnable service package.

required_facts.statement: Packages organize modules with qualified names such as package.module; regular packages contain an __init__.py file.
Import across a package with an absolute package-qualified import or a relative import using leading dots, whose meaning depends on the current package.
Run a module in its package context with python -m package.module; its __name__ is then __main__.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: As an orders service grows beyond one module, names should show which package owns each module. Running and importing code in that package context makes the qualified identity explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Packages organize modules with qualified names such as package.module; regular packages contain an __init__.py file.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Import across a package with an absolute package-qualified import or a relative import using leading dots, whose meaning depends on the current package. Run a module in its package context with python -m package.module; its __name__ is then __main__.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a regular service package containing __init__.py and a module called orders. Its qualified module name is service.orders. An absolute import names the package explicitly; a relative import uses leading dots whose meaning comes from the current package. Run the module in package context with python -m service.orders. In that execution its __name__ is __main__. Trace the same module in two roles: as a module referred to by its qualified package name, and as the module selected to run with -m. The distinction helps you read imports without treating each file as an unrelated top-level script. When choosing an import, ask what package context the leading dots refer to rather than counting directory separators as if that alone defined import meaning.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Relative imports depend on the current package. A file's location alone is not a substitute for understanding its package context.

video_need.reason: Annotated declarations and their resulting behavior make the input, ownership or contract boundary easier to follow. Focus: Organize an importable package: arrange one runnable service package.

practice_anchor.objective: Arrange service/__init__.py and service/orders.py as a regular package, identify service.orders as the qualified import name, and run orders in package context using python -m service.orders.
practice_anchor.success: The regular package contains __init__.py, service.orders is importable, and python -m service.orders runs successfully from the directory containing service. The learner identifies __main__ as the module's execution name.

live_code.required_skill: Organize a regular Python package, resolve its qualified module name, and select package-context execution.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an empty orders.py module and a service directory that is missing __init__.py. The learner places orders.py inside service, adds the regular-package marker, and supplies the qualified import and package-context execution command. No service endpoints or other application behavior are required.
live_code.observable_success: A supplied checker confirms that service/__init__.py and service/orders.py exist, importing service.orders succeeds, and python -m service.orders exits successfully from the parent directory. The learner records that __name__ is __main__ during that execution; no output-producing code is required.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show service/__init__.py and service/orders.py alongside the qualified import service.orders and the command python -m service.orders. Annotate the regular-package marker, the package context used by leading-dot imports, and the execution name __main__.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Packages establish qualified module identity.
Stay within the current objective: Organize an importable package. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Resolve package-qualified imports.

coverage.learning_objective: Enforce database constraints: declare one table's constraints.

required_facts.statement: Declare a column as TYPE NOT NULL to reject nulls independently of whether a write came through an application.
Declare UNIQUE (columns) to reject duplicate combinations; PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified.
Declare PRIMARY KEY (columns) for unique non-null row identity; a primary key can contain more than one column.
Declare FOREIGN KEY (columns) REFERENCES target (columns) so non-null referencing values must match referenced rows.
Declare CHECK (condition) to constrain values in a row; a check passes when its expression is true or null, so use NOT NULL separately when absence must be rejected.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An order rule should hold even when a database write comes from somewhere other than the API. Database constraints enforce row integrity at the stored-data boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a column as TYPE NOT NULL to reject nulls independently of whether a write came through an application.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Declare UNIQUE (columns) to reject duplicate combinations; PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified. Declare PRIMARY KEY (columns) for unique non-null row identity; a primary key can contain more than one column. Declare FOREIGN KEY (columns) REFERENCES target (columns) so non-null referencing values must match referenced rows. Declare CHECK (condition) to constrain values in a row; a check passes when its expression is true or null, so use NOT NULL separately when absence must be rejected.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Consider hypothetical orders with an identity, a customer reference and a quantity. A PRIMARY KEY supplies unique non-null row identity and may use multiple columns. A FOREIGN KEY requires non-null references to match referenced rows. For a quantity that must be present and satisfy a row condition, combine NOT NULL with CHECK rather than asking CHECK alone to reject absence. A check expression that is null passes, so the two declarations cover different cases. For an external reference that should be unique, UNIQUE rejects duplicate combinations, but PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct by default. If the requirement concerns null duplicates too, account for NULLS NOT DISTINCT. Work through one violating row at a time: null required value, duplicate identity, unmatched reference and failed condition. This identifies which constraint carries which rule instead of assuming application validation is the only place integrity lives.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: CHECK does not replace NOT NULL: true or null passes a check. PostgreSQL UNIQUE also treats nulls as distinct by default.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Enforce database constraints: declare one table's constraints.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete the supplied orders table declaration with a primary key on identity, a foreign key on customer_reference, NOT NULL and a positive-value CHECK on quantity, and UNIQUE on external_reference.
practice_anchor.success: The declaration gives orders unique non-null identity, requires non-null customer references to match existing customer identities, rejects absent or nonpositive quantities, and rejects duplicate non-null external references while retaining PostgreSQL's default distinct-null behavior.

live_code.required_skill: Declare database integrity constraints and distinguish the writes each constraint rejects.
allowed_syntax: Supplied INTEGER and TEXT column types
Parentheses, commas, and a terminating semicolon
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an unfinished CREATE TABLE orders declaration containing identity INTEGER, customer_reference INTEGER, quantity INTEGER, and external_reference TEXT. Supply editable constraint positions and state that customers already exists with identity as its primary key. No data-writing statements are needed.
live_code.observable_success: The completed declaration contains PRIMARY KEY (identity), FOREIGN KEY (customer_reference) REFERENCES customers (identity), quantity INTEGER NOT NULL, CHECK (quantity > 0), and UNIQUE (external_reference). It does not make customer_reference or external_reference mandatory or change the requested default unique-null policy.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show proposed orders rows beside the applicable constraint and acceptance or rejection outcome. Include null identity, duplicate identity, unmatched non-null customer reference, null customer reference, null quantity, nonpositive quantity, duplicate non-null external reference, and repeated null external references. Contrast CHECK alone with CHECK plus NOT NULL, and default UNIQUE behavior with NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Integrity holds independently of application callers.
Stay within the current objective: Enforce database constraints. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify rejected integrity-breaking writes.

clusters.title: Install and run a service package
clusters.reasoning: These adjacent concepts are complementary steps in preparing a runnable Python service: reconstruct its declared dependencies and organize and execute its importable package. Both require only the isolated-environment foundation already available at tile start. Dependency installation and package identity retain separate sub-concepts and exercises; neither is presented as a substitute for the other.
